  https://www.codyco.ai/

## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, it's obvious why Keel asks whether to collect the emails of people who say yes, and I do run pilots.
screens.why2: Pilot is my own word, and the hint says exactly what the respondent sees and where I see who said yes.
screens.why3: Offering a pilot is my decision and my go-to-market, so I can answer at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the whole choice, the two options are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a decision that is mine.
screens.why5: My pilot is a €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel that the director buys, whereas this line is a free-sounding email sign-up that doesn't say who it reaches, so the word has drifted a little from what I sell.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you try this at your hotel? Leave your email and we'll talk about the pilot." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out, picking who will put the questions to my reservation agents is an obvious last setup step, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question and the Daphne or Saskia choice are clear at once, but the hint packs in video, typing, credits, recording and text links, and "Keel records the voice you pick" needs a second read because the screen never shows a face and never says whether it is a person's look or only a voice.
screens.why3: I can answer by hearing both samples and judging which voice my agents and a German hotel group would listen to, and the 400 credits are a cost I can weigh myself.
screens.why4: Two distinct names with a 5-second sample and a preselected default are enough to choose, but nothing tells me whether either interviewer speaks German to agents in Germany, which is the thing I would pick on.
screens.why5: It keeps my "reservation agents" and my preselected pick stands as Daphne, with nothing of what I typed changed.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German on video? Daphne (picked for you) ▶ Hear her · Saskia ▶ Hear her. Recording your pick costs 400 credits either way; people get the link by text and can read and type or tap instead of talking.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks my reservation agents the questions, and just before sending, it is obvious why Keel wants to know how they will answer.
screens.why2: The choice is clear on a first read, but the Daphne option packs in a lot of detail, and its "Hear her" and "Still recording" text runs together and takes a second read to understand.
screens.why3: I know my agents work busy shifts, take calls and have phones or desktops at hand, so I can judge which format they would actually use.

AI interviewer (Daphne asks aloud on video; they talk, type or tap; ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (they read each question and tap or type; ready now) / Let them choose (they pick Daphne or read and tap when they open the link; ready in a few minutes)

screens.why1: Having chosen how the agents will be interviewed, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who gets a link.
screens.why2: The question and the three choices are plain on first reading, and the Contacts page is explained by the words around it.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching reservation agents I know by name, finding them by search or posting in a group where they already are.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach agents, and each says plainly what happens to the link.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is restated or changed, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as each person named with their own link.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title, and each card gives the deciding number against its bar (6 of 7, 5 of 7, 6 of 7, bar 5 of 7), with a line saying the verdict is the worst of the cards.
screens.why_b2: This page draws no chart, but each card's line plainly says what is counted, over 7 people, and where the bar sits at 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: The page gives me the verdict and tally but nothing on what it means for Codyco or what to do next, not even that relative advantage has no margin or that I should look at the 3 conditions on letting the AI answer.
screens.why_b5: The low n stays visible and "at the bar" and "3 on a condition" are said, but a flat "Holding up" over 7 people, with one belief exactly at the bar and half the AI yeses conditional, reads a little firmer than the data carries.
screens.instead: Holding up among the 7 who answered, but only just: relative advantage sits exactly at the bar and 3 of the 6 yeses on the AI come with a condition, so find out those conditions before you pitch a pilot.

screens.why_b1: The verdict "Holding up" sits directly beside its deciding number, 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: On first look I can see that it counts the agents' answers on forwarding, over 7 people, with the bar at 5 and the 6 for clearing it.
screens.why_b3: The name Compatibility and the line about forwarding unanswered calls to another number are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely that call forwarding is not the blocker among these people and sends me to Adoption friction as the thing to work on next.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 7 people and "a lean, not a call", but the So line flatly states what "will stop them" and that Adoption friction is it, which is firmer than seven answers can carry.
screens.instead: Among these 7, forwarding doesn't look like the blocker, though Aylin's old phone system would need IT and an owner willing to pay; Adoption friction, below, looks like the bigger risk.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "5 of 7 said it would have gone better" and "bar 5 of 7, at the bar", so I see both the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: At first look I can see the question being counted, the 5 better, 1 same and 1 worse over 7 people, and the bar at 5 of 7, which the strip's marker repeats.
screens.why_b3: The name Relative advantage and the line about missed calls turning into bookings are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the 5 of 7 and points me to Adoption friction, but doesn't say what this means for the idea, such as that it just reaches the bar and that a call center or a guest wanting a person is where the benefit stops.
screens.why_b5: It says "at the bar", "a small group: a lean, not a call", "a hypothetical" and "imagined", keeps the 7 visible and makes no claim beyond these people.
screens.instead: 5 of 7 imagined their last shift going better, exactly at your bar, so one answer the other way would drop it: this is a lean to test on a real shift in a pilot, and the two against are a group whose call center already covers after hours and an agent whose guests want a person, so check whether those hotels are really yours before you pitch them.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7", so I know the belief held and which number decides it, and that 3 of the 6 came with a condition.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each answer (3 yes, 3 yes if worth it, 0 probably not, 1 no) over the 7 who answered, and the bar at 5 of 7 is named and marked on the strip, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The name Adoption friction and the line about letting an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice are the ones I checked, though "You said let an AI answer..." reads as a clipped fragment.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the 3 conditional yeses are what to look at, but it promises what would make it worth it to them "below" and below are only names and their picks, so I learn no condition and no concrete step for my pilot.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called "a lean, not a call", and the 3 conditional yeses are split out rather than presented as firm support.
screens.instead: Holding up, 6 of 7 on a small group, but only 3 said a plain yes; Murat, Chiara and Aylin would do it if it was clearly worth it, and here is what each said would make it so, so show them that before asking them to let the AI answer in your hotel's voice.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on Holding up with the deciding number beside it (6 of 7 against a bar of 5, and 5 of 7 at the bar), and the line above the quotes repeats the verdict.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Relative advantage carry the names and belief lines I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: The screen never says what these answers mean for the idea, so I must work out for myself that old phone systems and groups whose call center already covers evenings could shape who I sell to first.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and at the bar is said, but 'the 1 who said no' covers an answer tagged Only sometimes, and 'held' is not qualified as resting on just 7 people, with Relative advantage having no margin.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I did not type: an old phone system that needs IT and an owner who won't pay to replace it, a call center that already covers after six while group requests eat the day, and guests who ring for a person who knows the house.
screens.instead: Relative advantage is at the bar with only 7 people, and the 2 against point to where to look next: groups whose call center already covers evenings and houses whose guests ring for a person, while Aylin's old phone system shows forwarding can need IT and an owner's money, so check these before picking pilot hotels.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it makes sense to check whether my workplace has a central reservations office before asking about my calls.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call center are everyday words in my job, so I can answer at first reading.
screens.why3: I work in the Munich central office, so I know for certain that my hotel group runs one.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for this factual question, and a screener needs no escape.
screens.why5: It asks only about my employer's setup and shows nothing of any product, plan or founder's terms for people.
screens.why6: It is one short question with a two-option list that is easy to hold after hearing it once.

screens.why1: After asking about our central office, it makes sense to check whether I took booking calls this week before asking me about a specific call.
screens.why2: "Booking call" and "shift" are the words we use every day, so I can answer at once, although it is almost too obvious because calls come in on every shift.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I worked this week and whether calls came in, because that is my job.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but "I can't recall one particular shift" is odd because the question covers any shift in the week, and "I'd rather not say" is pointless on such a harmless question.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or company reaches me; it only asks about calls on my shift.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it is one short question followed by "Yes or no", which I can hear once and answer straight away.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call come in on your shift? Yes / No (no escape chips)

screens.why1: Part 2 is marked as an idea to consider, and after being asked about booking calls on my shift it is clear why I am now shown an idea about calls that go unanswered.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot, Apaleo, forwarding calls and handing calls to the desk are everyday words in my reservations office, so I understand it on first reading.
screens.why3: It describes my own work of booking calls, payment, confirmations and handovers to the desk, so I can picture it from what I do on a busy Saturday.
screens.why4: The screen is a card to read and shows no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: It is an openly shown idea card, and its product wording reaches me on purpose and in terms my trade uses, with no founder-only language where it should not be.
screens.why6: It can be followed when heard, but it is long for one hearing, the system list OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo is a small mouthful, and the belief repeats the how instead of pointing back to it as §17 asks.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, AI answering for missed calls. Your hotel forwards calls nobody picks up to Codyco, an AI reservation agent. It answers the guest's questions in your hotel's voice, takes the payment and writes the confirmed booking straight into your PMS. It hands calls to your desk by your hotel's rules. The people building it believe this would turn those missed calls into bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea of AI answering for missed calls, it makes sense to ask whether my missed calls could actually be sent somewhere else.
screens.why2: Forwarding calls is everyday language at a reservations desk, but "your unanswered calls" and "could you have" leave me a moment unsure whether they mean my phone rights, the system's setup or what is allowed.
screens.why3: I know how to transfer a single caller and what my login shows, but whether unanswered calls can be diverted to another number is usually set by the ACD or IT, so I would partly guess for a central office.
screens.why4: The options are clear and the escape fits, but "most of the time" and "only sometimes" read oddly on a yes-or-no question about what the phone system allows, because it either can or cannot.
screens.why5: It asks about my own calls and my own shift in ordinary words, and nothing of the founder's plan reaches me beyond the idea card shown on purpose.
screens.why6: It is one short anchor and one short question, followed by four short options and one escape, so I could hear it once and answer.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift. Could you have sent calls nobody picked up to another number yourself? Yes; yes, but only with a supervisor or IT; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and a question about my last shift, it makes sense to ask whether this thing would have helped on that shift.
screens.why2: Short plain words I get on first reading; the card's "AI answering for missed calls" tells me enough to know what Codyco is, and missed calls is how we talk at the desk too.
screens.why3: I know how my last shift went and how many calls got away, but the card gives only one line, so I would partly be guessing how well an AI would handle a guest asking about a trade-fair rate.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from a lot better to worse, they are distinct and in my words, and I can't tell fits since I have never seen it work.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose, and the name Codyco is only there because the card introduced it.
screens.why6: Heard once it is one short question with four short options I can hold, and the escape comes last and is easy to say.

screens.why1: After the idea card and the question on whether it would have helped my shift, it makes sense to ask if I would actually let the AI take calls.
screens.why2: I understand the question at once, but "in your hotel's voice" makes me stop, because I work for a group's central office and don't know if it means a real-sounding voice, our greeting or our way of speaking.
screens.why3: I can say how I feel about an AI taking my guests' calls, but the group's management would decide this rather than an agent like me, so "you'd let" is partly a guess.
screens.why4: The four answers run clearly from yes to no in words I would use, and "I can't tell" fits if I don't know enough about it.
screens.why5: The AI on the card is shown on purpose, but "in your hotel's voice" sounds like the company's sales phrase rather than something anyone in our office would say.
screens.why6: Heard once it is short, one question with four short options and one escape at the end, so I could answer straight away.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, an AI would answer the guest calls nobody at your office picks up, using your hotel's name. Would you be fine with that, or not? Yes; Yes, if it was clearly worth it; Probably not; No; I can't tell.
